h: פָּרָשַׁת הַחֹדֶשׁ, מַאֲמָר ט׳ Parshas HaChodesh — Maamar Tes

p: "They shall take for themselves, each man,
a lamb for the father's house,
In the Pesikta on Parshas HaChodesh
"'They shall take for themselves, a man' —
whom you take through the two tamid offerings;
'a lamb' — this is the tamid offering," etc.
כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב וְגוֹמֵר [מִשְׁלֵי ד, ב]
"'For I have given you a good teaching, etc.' (Mishlei 4:2):
I have sold you My Torah,
and, as it were, I was sold with it,
'And let them take for Me an offering.'
make for Me one small chamber
so that I may dwell among you," etc.,
And this is what they said,
"whom you take through the two tamid offerings,"
for of them it is written (Bamidbar 28:2):
"My offering, My bread for My fire-offerings";
And this is "let them take for Me":
that He dwells with them, as mentioned above.
And immediately when they were told
being the beginning of the words of Torah,
they were told, "They shall take for themselves a man" —
that is, "as it were, I was sold with it,"
so that I may dwell among you."
And even though there was not yet
the heart of Yisrael is a dwelling for the Shechinah,
as they said in the Pesikta (there, siman 6)
and my portion is God forever."
And even though there was not then
the lintel and the two doorposts
"This is the law of the olah, etc.,"
"This is the law of the chatas":
whoever engages in the laws of the chatas
is as if he offered a chatas.
are always a dwelling for the Shechinah,
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג כט, ב)
and their heart is a dwelling for the Shechinah,
that one makes a beautiful dwelling (dirah)
for the Shechinah in his heart
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּיקּוּן ו כב, ב)
And then is the spreading of
"the shelter of peace over us," etc.,
for they merit the holiness of Yerushalayim,
and the heart of Yisrael is a dwelling for the Shechinah.
And the Torah is "Come, eat of My bread":
which are "My bread for My fire-offerings."
corresponding to the upper and the lower Shechinah.
who makes for them a dwelling on Shabbos
in the two chambers of the heart," etc.
in Pesikta Rabbasi and Shir HaShirim Rabbah
from what is written, "The Rock of my heart, etc."
And this is the latter Elokim
"And if I am a Master, where is My fear?" —
the speculum that does not shine,
through which the work of the world is done
And throughout the work of Creation
עַל מִי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם
about one who has no fear of Heaven:
"Then you will understand the fear of Hashem";
that is, when the fear enters
into the depth of the point within the heart,
that is the aspect of "Binah is the heart."
as they said in the holy Zohar
and therefore it is called the Supernal Rock";
"From the side of the Supernal Rock
אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָאו אִיהִי דִּינָא
from her side it is found," etc.
is "dina" — "the law of the kingdom is law" —
the Name Adnus with its letters reversed
And this is "there issues another rock."
And at the beginning of the Torah,
which is the section "This month shall be for you,"
they were told, "They shall take for themselves a man":
and later merited to make a Mishkan,
it is written "Let them take for Me," as mentioned above.
And this is what it says:
"whom you take through the two tamid offerings."
And about this it is said:
"a lamb for the father's house, a lamb for the household";
and this is what is written in the Pesikta
in Yerushalayim with sin in his hand:
for sins committed by day," etc.
And this is what is said:
which atones for the sins of the day,
committed through the company of people;
which atones for the sins of the night
and this is "a lamb for the household."
And the Pesikta concludes: What is the reason?
That is, Tzedek, the holy Malchus;
and that is "Let them take for Me,"
so that I may dwell among you."
"Open for me the gates of righteousness,"
the righteous shall enter through it."
For to enter the gates of Tzedek,
And this is what he expounded:
וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן צֶדֶק יָלִין בָּהּ
and through that, "Tzedek lodges in her":

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Bas Ayin, Terumah, citing the Alshich — “‘And I will dwell in their midst’: it does not say ‘in its midst’ but ‘in their midst,’ teaching that HaKadosh Baruch Hu dwells within each and every one of Yisrael.” The Chassidic reading reaches the same principle from the verse of the Mishkan. The building is secondary. The true dwelling is the heart of each Jew, and so it existed even before there was a Mishkan.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 96a — “Rav Yosef taught: There were three altars there—upon the lintel and upon the two doorposts—and there was nothing else.” The discussion concerns the blood of the Pesach offering in Egypt and whether any portion belonged on an altar. The lintel and two doorposts provide the three places of application to which Rav Tzadok refers.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 29b, Tzav — “So Torah scholars, the children of the King and the Queen, are called Shabbosos and festivals. They have nothing of their own, for they are not craftsmen like the other servants, the children of the ordinary weekdays. Their reward in this world and the world to come is that they be delighted with every kind of food and drink and honored with fine garments, like Shabbos, of which it is said: ‘Honor it with clean clothing.’ Everything a person does for Shabbosos and festivals he must do for them.” The 29b marker stands in the preceding paragraph. The analogy here is stated through the scholars’ sacred status and the honor given them; Rav Tzadok develops the correspondence through the Shechinah’s dwelling.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar 22b — “When the Shechinah is in exile, it is said of her, ‘The dove found no resting place,’ except on Shabbos and festivals. At that time she unites with her husband, and many additional souls descend with her to dwell in Israel. This is what is written: ‘The children of Israel shall keep Shabbos ... for their generations.’ Fortunate is one who prepares for her a beautiful dwelling in his heart, beautiful vessels in his limbs, and a beautiful wife, which is his soul; on its account the supernal Shechinah, the soul of all living, rests upon him.” The passage interprets ledorosam through the language of dwelling. It gives the heart, limbs, and soul as the human setting of that dwelling, which Rav Tzadok places alongside the physical Sanctuary.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 31b, Bereishis — “Rabbi Yosei said: What is meant by ‘Which has gods near to it’? Should it not have said ‘near’ in the singular? Rather: the supernal Elokim, the Elokim of the fear of Yitzchak, and the final Elokim. Therefore it says ‘near’ in the plural. There are many mighty powers that emerge from one, and all are one.” The 31b marker occurs earlier in the chapter. The Zohar distinguishes several applications of the same divine name while maintaining their unity. Rav Tzadok invokes the final application in speaking of the indwelling attribute.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 172a, Vayishlach — “‘At the pace of the work’—what is the work? This is the mirror that does not shine, through which the work of the world is performed. ‘Which is before me’—this is what is meant everywhere by ‘from before Hashem.’ ‘And at the pace of the children’—this is the mystery of the cherubs, to show the mystery of faith to which he cleaved.” The interpretation is of Yaakov’s words in Bereishis 33:14. The non-shining mirror receives rather than originating its light; Rav Tzadok connects this receptive aspect with the divine action within creation. The preceding chapter 9 carries 172a.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 72b — “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonasan’s name: What is meant by ‘Why is there a price in the fool’s hand to acquire wisdom, while there is no heart’? Woe to the enemies of Torah scholars who occupy themselves with Torah but have no fear of Heaven. Rabbi Yannai proclaimed: Woe to one who has no courtyard, yet makes a gate for his courtyard!” “The enemies of Torah scholars” is the Gemara’s indirect expression for the people being criticized. The exposition makes the absence of “heart” a lack of reverence despite learning, which is the connection Rav Tzadok requires.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 64a–b, Beshalach — “Rabbi Abba said: There is a rock and there is a rock. From the side of the supernal rock another rock emerges. What is the supernal rock? The rock of all rocks. What is it? That which gave birth to Israel, as it is written, ‘You weakened the Rock who bore you.’ From the side of the supernal rock above, another rock emerges; from the side of the Mother, Gevurah emerges. ... ‘Who can utter the mighty acts of Hashem?’—this includes the supernal Mother of all. Although she is not judgment, it is found from her side, for from her side Gevurah is found; therefore she is called the supernal rock.” The wording crosses the embedded boundary from 64a into 64b. The distinction between the maternal source and the Gevurah emerging from it explains Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the two rocks and two levels of reverence.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 118a, Mishpatim — “Rise and awaken in judgments. The Faithful Shepherd opened: ‘Adonai, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare Your praise.’ Adonai, with its letters rearranged, is dina, judgment. Therefore the masters of the Mishnah said: ‘The law of kingship is law.’ All judgments are judged through this name. ... The middle column is the true judge: he judges from the side of Adonai, where he is the true judge; from the side of the name Elokim, he is called judge, as it is written, ‘For Elokim is judge.’” The 118a marker occurs in the preceding chapter 14. The exact rearrangement of the divine name into dina is explicit; Rav Tzadok uses it to explain the royal aspect’s relation to judgment.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tzav 3 — on “no one ever spent the night in Yerushalayim with sin in his hand”: “The olah comes only for the thoughts of the heart (Vayikra Rabbah 7), and the Zohar says the olah is for evil thought.” This explains how a tamid can atone at all. The sins it covers are those of the heart, and they come most of all when a person is alone in his house at night.
